claims.text: Low defaults reduce average donation amounts (the 'scale-back' effect).
Defaulting a low amount increases the donation rate (the 'lower-bar' effect).
Introducing any defaults reduces the effect of other cues, such as positive charity information (the 'default-distraction' effect).
Defaults increased overall revenue in the natural field study.
Defaults can act as a self-canceling intervention where countervailing effects of default option magnitude lead to no net effect on revenue.

evidence.description: Demonstrated across eight studies comprising 11,508 participants making 2,423 donation decisions.
Observed across eight studies examining choice-option defaults on donation rate.
Observed in experimental testing evaluating the interaction between defaults and other cues like positive charity information.
Reported from a large-scale natural field experiment evaluating the effect of defaults on total revenue.
Derived from the combined experimental and field evidence on donation rates versus average amounts across different default magnitudes.

methodologies.name: Experimental and natural field experiments on choice-option defaults
methodologies.description: Eight studies, including experimental settings and a large-scale natural field experiment, testing default donation amounts among 11,508 participants making 2,423 donation decisions.
conditions: presence of positive charity information cues

limitations.text: Defaults can produce countervailing effects on donation decisions that result in no net effect on revenue.
Prior view held that setting defaults in charitable appeals will backfire.
